title: {{NAME}} and the Night the Garden Held Its Breath
moral: Even the most powerful hero learns that the greatest strength is knowing when to slow down and listen.

pages.content: The Guardian Garden was the size of a city block and older than any map. Every species of plant that existed, and several that had been presumed extinct, grew there in careful, tended order, the whole thing maintained by the Fairy Groundskeepers who had worked it for generations. {{NAME}} arrived at a run, his indigo cape streaming behind him, silver heels striking the garden path with a sound like small bells. Something had triggered the garden's emergency signal: a deep, subsonic pulse that only certain people and most animals could hear, and {{NAME}} had felt it as far away as the eastern ridge. He vaulted the iron gate and landed in the central pathway. The garden was completely still. Not asleep-still, not peaceful-still, but the specific stillness of something holding its breath because it is afraid. Every flower was closed. Every bird had gone. The hedges stood at attention like soldiers. The only movement was a small cluster of fairy-lights far ahead, deep in the rose section, flaring and dimming with the urgency of distress signals. {{NAME}} began to run again, then stopped himself. Something about the garden's held breath told him that speed was, for once, exactly the wrong tool.

pages.content: Walking instead of running through a garden that needed help was one of the harder things {{NAME}} had done. He counted his breaths and kept his hands open at his sides, non-threatening, the way you approach an animal that needs to decide on its own whether to trust you. The fairy-lights grew brighter as he approached, and he began to make out the scene. Three fairies, each no bigger than his thumb, were attempting to contain something that was too large to be contained by three thumbs. A young barn owl, ivory-white and enormous-eyed, had landed in the middle of the heritage rose beds, and she was caught. Her left wing was tangled in a web of fine thorns, the kind that grew from the oldest rose stock, black-stemmed and needle-precise. She had pulled and pulled until the thorns had tightened, and now any movement hurt. The three fairies, whose names turned out to be Thistle, Burr, and Pip, had been talking to her in calm, methodical rotation for two hours, keeping her still, preventing the panic that would cause real damage. Their eyes found {{NAME}}'s and the relief in them was vivid and immediate.

pages.content: He did not touch the thorns first. He sat down in the rose bed, cross-legged, at exactly the owl's eye level, and he waited. The owl looked at him with one enormous amber eye, the pupil a dark well. She was trembling finely, the trembling of sustained fear rather than cold. Thistle landed on {{NAME}}'s shoulder and murmured the owl's name: Sable. {{NAME}} said it, once, quietly. Sable's other eye opened. He said nothing else. He just stayed, cape pooled around him, still as the closed flowers, present without pressure. It was the fairies who had told him this without telling him: they had been talking, not doing, for two hours, because talking was what was needed before doing could help. After four minutes that felt considerably longer, Sable stopped trembling. Her feathers settled. {{NAME}} reached forward with both hands, slow as a minute hand, and began unpicking thorns from flight feathers one by one, each one requiring its own careful angle, its own particular patience. Thistle and Burr guided his fingers by touch, and Pip kept up a constant, low, musical hum that kept Sable still.

pages.content: The last thorn was the deepest, set at an angle that required {{NAME}} to hold his breath and work by touch alone. Burr had her hands flat against his fingertips, and for that minute the three fairies and the superhero and the owl were all perfectly synchronised, a single still point in the middle of the enormous garden. Then the thorn came free. Sable spread her wing wide, testing it, and the movement was like a sail filling: slow, then sudden, all the latent power of the wing remembering what it was for. She looked at {{NAME}} once more with that amber eye, and what was in it now was different from before. Not fear. Not even relief. Something older and quieter: recognition. Then she launched upward from the rose bed in a silent, powerful surge, white against the darkening sky, and climbed until she was a pale point between the first stars. The garden exhaled. {{NAME}} felt it: every flower opening a fraction, every hedge relaxing its posture by a degree. The breath that had been held for hours, finally let out. Thistle sat on his knee and cried, very briefly, and then was loudly indignant about it.

pages.content: The garden reopened slowly over the next hour, the way a person relaxes after a long held tension, petal by petal, hedge by hedge, bird by returning bird. The fairy groundskeepers came back to their work, checking roots and stems with the professional briskness of people who had taken an unexpected break and had opinions about it. Thistle had recovered her composure entirely and was writing a formal incident report on a leaf the size of a stamp. Burr was already replanting a section of rose that had been disturbed. Only Pip sat still, up on the garden wall, watching Sable's pale shape circle high above the darkening garden, endlessly patient, as if waiting to see where she would go. {{NAME}} found the warmest corner of the garden, near the old stone wall where the stones held the day's heat until well after midnight, and sat with his back against it, indigo cape around his shoulders like a blanket. His eyes went slow. The stars arranged themselves above him, orderly and bright. He was asleep before Sable's first hunting call rang out across the garden, clear and sure and completely free. But somewhere in the garden, something else had started to untangle itself, quietly and on its own.
